lessons.title: Principles of precision agriculture
lessons.html:
From field averages to managing variability

Traditional farming treats a field as uniform: one seeding rate, one fertiliser rate, one spray programme. In reality, soil depth, texture, water-holding capacity, pH, nutrient levels, weed pressure and yield potential vary greatly within a single land, especially on the variable sandy and duplex soils common across South African grain areas. Precision agriculture is a management approach that measures this variability and responds to it, applying the right input, at the right rate, in the right place, at the right time.

The precision farming cycle

  1. Collect data: GNSS-referenced yield maps, soil sampling grids or zones, electrical conductivity surveys, satellite and drone imagery, weather stations, soil moisture probes.
  2. Analyse and interpret: identify patterns that are stable over years, separate causes (soil, drainage, compaction, pests) from noise.
  3. Make decisions: define management zones and prescriptions.
  4. Apply: variable-rate seeding, fertiliser, lime, irrigation and spraying; auto-steer and section control.
  5. Evaluate: compare results against expectations and refine.

Where the value comes from

  • Reducing inputs where they will not pay (for example lowering seed and nitrogen on shallow, low-potential soils)
  • Raising inputs where yield potential justifies it
  • Cutting overlaps and skips with guidance and section control, saving seed, fertiliser, chemicals and diesel
  • Correcting limiting factors, such as patchy acidity, with variable-rate lime
  • Better records for traceability, audits and financing

Limitations

Technology does not replace agronomy. Poor data, uncalibrated sensors, or zones drawn without ground-truthing lead to expensive mistakes. Benefits depend on how variable the field actually is; a very uniform field gains little from variable-rate application. Connectivity in rural areas, data compatibility between brands, and the skills to interpret data are real constraints. This qualification develops the ability to select and apply precision tools critically, rather than adopting technology for its own sake.

lessons.title: Data sources and technologies
lessons.html:
Positioning

Almost all precision tools depend on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS), of which GPS is one. Accuracy ranges from a few metres with an uncorrected receiver to around two centimetres with real-time kinematic (RTK) correction from a base station or network. Auto-steer for planting and controlled traffic requires high accuracy; yield mapping and scouting can work with lower accuracy.

Measuring the field

ToolWhat it showsNotes
Yield monitorYield and moisture across the fieldNeeds calibration each season and crop; clean data before use
Grid or zone soil samplingpH, acidity, P, K and other nutrients by locationSample density and laboratory consistency are critical
Soil EC surveyDifferences in texture, depth, salinityGood basis for zones; must be ground-truthed with pits or auger samples
Satellite imagery (NDVI and other indices)Crop vigour and its change in timeCloud cover can limit; low cost per hectare
DronesHigh-resolution imagery, plant counts, spot detectionCivil aviation rules apply to commercial use; operators need appropriate licensing
Soil moisture probes and weather stationsWater status, rainfall, evapotranspirationKey for irrigation scheduling

Applying inputs

  • Guidance and auto-steer: reduces overlap and operator fatigue; enables controlled traffic.
  • Section and row control: switches planter rows or boom sections off over areas already covered.
  • Variable-rate technology (VRT): controllers read a prescription map and adjust rates on the go.
  • Variable-rate irrigation: on centre pivots, varies application by sector or nozzle zone.
  • Targeted spraying: camera-based systems that spray only weeds detected in fallow or between rows.

Data management

Data from different machines and service providers often comes in different formats. Use a farm management information system that can import common formats, keep field boundaries consistent, and store data securely. Agree in writing with service providers who owns and may use the farm's data. Handle any personal information of employees or clients according to the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013.

lessons.title: Selecting, applying and evaluating precision tools
lessons.html:
Building management zones

A management zone is an area within a field that has similar yield-limiting factors and therefore should receive similar treatment. Robust zones combine several layers: multi-year yield maps (normalised so different seasons can be compared), soil EC, elevation, imagery and farmer knowledge. Ground-truth every zone with soil pits or samples before writing prescriptions. Typically two to five zones per field are practical.

Writing prescriptions

Prescriptions should be based on agronomic response, not only on maps. For example, a variable-rate nitrogen plan uses the expected yield and response in each zone; a seeding prescription lowers plant population on low-potential soils where moisture limits yield. Use the recommendations of a qualified agronomist, soil laboratory and seed company, and always keep the rates within product label limits for any agricultural remedies under Act 36 of 1947.

Selecting technology

QuestionWhy it matters
How variable are my fields?Determines potential return from VRT
What decision will this data improve?Avoid collecting data that changes nothing
Is it compatible with my machinery and software?Avoid isolated systems
What support and training is available locally?Downtime at planting is costly
What is the payback?Capital, subscriptions and labour against savings and yield gains

On-farm trials and evaluation

Test prescriptions with strip or checkerboard trials: alternate standard and variable rates across zones, harvest with a calibrated yield monitor, and compare yield and gross margin per hectare. Repeat over seasons, because one season's rainfall can dominate results.

Economic analysis

Calculate the investment (receivers, controllers, subscriptions, sampling, consulting) and annual savings (seed, fertiliser, chemicals, fuel, labour) plus any yield or quality gains. Consider shared ownership or contracting where the farm is small. Report results in rand per hectare to support management decisions.

Key points

  • Precision agriculture measures in-field variability and manages inputs to match it.
  • Accurate positioning, calibrated sensors and clean data are the foundation.
  • Build zones from several data layers and ground-truth them.
  • Choose technology based on the decision it improves and its payback.
  • Evaluate with on-farm trials over several seasons and express results in rand per hectare.
